content: The studies excluded from the analysis were those that focused on screening in blood banks and healthcare workers unless they also reported subsequent linkage to care and treatment. Evaluations involving screening prior to vaccination were excluded unless they also considered antiviral therapy for individuals identified as HBsAg-positive. Studies examining HBV screening before chemotherapy were excluded as they were deemed relevant only to high-income settings and a small subset of populations in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Additionally, studies addressing co-infection with HIV or comparing diagnostic methods were excluded. The PubMed search identified 32 studies, many of which overlapped with bibliographies from existing reviews. All studies were conducted in high-income countries (HICs), and no prior studies were found that described the cost or cost-effectiveness of HBV screening in LMICs. Ultimately, eight published studies and one unpublished study met the inclusion criteria and are discussed in detail. The existing literature on the cost-effectiveness of HBV screening and treatment has primarily been conducted in HICs, where the general population prevalence of HBV is low. The discussion also includes unpublished PROLIFICA data, which represents the only study conducted in a low-income country (LIC) setting. Two studies evaluated HBV screening in the general population, while seven studies focused on high-risk groups, most of which involved screening in migrant or refugee populations. Studies on antenatal care (ANC) screening were excluded as they did not consider antiviral therapy for mothers and only assessed the benefits of screening to guide vaccination strategies for reducing mother-to-child transmission. The studies employed various screening methods for high-risk groups, including clinical settings, community outreach, and overseas screening. Outcome measures included cost per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) gained, cost per life-year (LY) saved, and cost per case screened. Many models used hypothetical cohorts. For example, one U.S. study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of HBsAg testing in asymptomatic outpatients in primary care settings, using a hypothetical cohort of 35-year-old males with a 2% HBV prevalence. Screening followed by treatment with one of four regimens was found to be cost-effective, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of $29,230/QALY. A forthcoming study in The Gambia and Senegal screened nearly 10,000 adults for HBsAg at the community level using active outreach. Those testing positive underwent clinical assessment and antiviral treatment if eligible. This study reported an ICER of $705/LY gained, $476/QALY gained, or $575/disability-adjusted life-year (DALY) averted, compared to the status quo. The authors acknowledged the debate surrounding willingness-to-pay (WTP) thresholds in LMICs. This is the only cost-effectiveness study of HBV screening and treatment identified in LMIC settings, and it provides real-life cost and effectiveness data from a large-scale intervention program. Six studies examined the cost-effectiveness of screening and treatment in migrant or refugee populations in HICs, and one study analyzed screening all high-risk groups in Italy. For instance, a Canadian study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of screening and treating immigrants for chronic hepatitis B (CHB) using a case-finding strategy during primary care visits. The screen-and-treat strategy had an ICER of $69,000/QALY gained, which was within the WTP range of $50,000 to $120,000 for Canada. However, the model assumed high uptake and adherence rates, which may not be realistic. Another Canadian study assessed various scenarios involving screening, treatment, and vaccination among newly arrived immigrants and refugees. The screen-and-treat scenario was the most cost-effective, with an ICER of $40,880/QALY gained, though it exceeded the $50,000/QALY WTP threshold when HBsAg prevalence was below 3%. A societal perspective was used, with baseline assumptions of 70% screening acceptance, 60% linkage to care, and 75% treatment adherence. An earlier U.S. study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of screening and vaccinating Asian Pacific Islander adults for HBV using a hypothetical cohort with a 10% HBsAg prevalence. The screen-and-treat strategy was the most cost-effective, with an ICER of $36,000/QALY gained, even at a 1% HBsAg prevalence. This study also adopted a societal perspective. A more recent U.S. study compared the cost-benefits of two overseas programs for reducing HBV infection among refugees: vaccination only versus screening and vaccination, with onward treatment in the U.S. for HBsAg-positive individuals. The study utilized original datasets from refugee populations in two U.S. states and assumed 100% screening adherence, 60% linkage to specialist care, and 90% treatment adherence. A European study analyzed the cost-effectiveness of HBV screening and early treatment of migrants using an active screening method. The target population was identified through municipal population registries and invited via mail to attend screening. Screening and treatment had an ICER of €8,966/QALY saved, which was cost-effective compared to the WTP threshold of €20,000/QALY. Variations in linkage to care and treatment adherence significantly influenced the ICER. Another U.S. study described different methods of HBV screening among Asian migrants, including community clinic testing and active outreach at community events. Costs per person screened ranged from $40 to $280, with clinic-based screening being the least costly but reaching fewer individuals. Active outreach was more expensive but reached more people. This study highlighted the relative costs of various screening methods but did not provide long-term outcomes following a positive screening test. A study in Italy evaluated the cost-effectiveness of screening all high-risk groups, as defined by local guidelines, followed by treatment for CHB using one of five antiviral drugs. Screening and treatment had an ICER of €17,000/QALY compared to the status quo of no screening and treatment only at advanced disease stages. Screening pregnant women for HBsAg in ANC settings has been considered in previous cost-effectiveness analyses. However, these studies focused solely on reducing mother-to-child transmission and benefits to the child, without addressing onward care or treatment for the mother to reduce her risk of liver disease progression. Many of these studies are older and conducted in HICs, limiting their relevance to current recommendations for HBV screening and treatment in ANC settings in LMICs. Key drivers of cost-effectiveness for HBV screening and treatment strategies include baseline HBsAg prevalence, costs of screening, diagnostics, monitoring, and drugs, as well as adherence to treatment and linkage to care. While HBsAg prevalence had a relatively small influence on cost-effectiveness across wide ranges, the analyses consistently showed that screen-and-treat strategies remained cost-effective even at low prevalence levels. This finding has important implications for strategy selection in countries with varying prevalence profiles. The cost of antiviral drugs was a significant driver of cost-effectiveness in some studies. For example, the PROLIFICA study used a generic tenofovir price of $48, which is available for HIV programs in sub-Saharan Africa, but not for HBV mono-infection. Using the current pharmaceutical price of $207 increased the ICER but remained below the WTP threshold. Screening costs varied widely, with active outreach strategies being more expensive but reaching more individuals. Adherence to treatment and linkage to care were critical factors influencing cost-effectiveness. For instance, variations in linkage and adherence rates significantly impacted ICERs in several studies. These findings underscore the importance of ensuring high rates of linkage to care and treatment adherence to maximize the cost-effectiveness of HBV screening and treatment programs.
